assumptions: The score assumes a recurring commercial need among EEG and sleep-device teams for credible protocol-based validation, while treating willingness to join a shared consortium as unproven.

The model receives no near-term or exclusive data-access advantage from EHDS; all useful cross-sponsor benchmark rights must instead be granted lawfully through specific contracts, participant documentation, and the applicable regulatory process.

Qualified clinic, principal-investigator, privacy, and quality roles perform the regulated and participant-facing work rather than the founder attempting to cover those duties alongside full-time employment.
No cohort launches unless sponsor deposits cover the contracted external costs, so the 175000 PLN project estimate is not assumed to be founder-funded.
evidence_needed_for_higher_score: A higher score requires a named clinic and qualified clinical team under costed responsibility terms, a documented protocol-specific regulatory route, at least two noncompeting sponsors signing and paying deposits for the same endpoint, legal confirmation of the proposed derived-benchmark reuse rights, a quoted cohort budget showing attractive contribution margin and cash timing, and evidence of repeat or renewal demand after the first protocol.

factors.name: Core insight
factors.rationale: Pooling a fixed reference protocol across noncompeting device sponsors could amortize cohort and clinical-operation costs while producing more comparable validation outputs. The precommitment gates sharpen the concept, but the insight depends on sponsors accepting the same endpoint, timing, and governance rather than commissioning private work.

factors.name: Customer pain and willingness to pay
factors.rationale: A device or algorithm release can create a consequential need for credible comparison against clinician labels and a stable protocol, and incumbent CRO offerings support the existence of paid demand for validation. The packet does not establish that buyers value a shared Central-European benchmark, will coordinate with another sponsor, or will prepay at a viable price.

factors.name: Business model and economics
factors.rationale: Deposits before launch improve cash conversion and cap founder exposure, while standardized analytics and permitted benchmark access could add operating leverage beyond a one-off study. However, clinic, recruitment, insurance, regulatory, support, secure-compute, and biostatistics costs are unquoted; price, gross margin, sales cycle, renewal, and lawful recurring benchmark revenue are all unknown, leaving the model close to a bespoke service until proven otherwise.

factors.name: Market and beachhead
factors.rationale: EEG or sleep-device teams sharing one endpoint form a coherent and operationally focused initial segment. That narrowness helps protocol consistency, but the number of sponsors with synchronized validation needs and willingness to share benchmark terms may be too small or episodic to support a meaningful beachhead on its own.

factors.name: Competitive position and domination potential
factors.rationale: A repeat clinic protocol and a uniquely governed local reference cohort could support a defensible niche. VivoSense, Empatica, TNO, and Delve already cover substantial portions of the protocol, device, analytics, regulatory, quality-control, and participant-operations stack, and no exclusive clinic access or buyer preference establishes a path to dominance.

factors.name: Expansion potential
factors.rationale: A successful first endpoint could lead to device-version updates, additional sponsors, adjacent sleep or EEG endpoints, and access to permitted derived reference metrics. Each new endpoint may require fresh protocol, regulatory, clinic, and data-right work, so expansion is plausible but not automatically low-cost or cumulative.

factors.name: Defensibility and durability
factors.rationale: Documented reuse rights, accumulated comparable measurements, protocol failure modes, and clinic repetition could compound into a useful data and workflow asset. The necessary reuse rights are unresolved, small cohorts may have limited benchmark value, and well-capitalized CROs or platforms could reproduce the operating approach if demand becomes visible.

factors.name: Strength of advantage
factors.rationale: Shared funding may offer sponsors lower cost and a more comparable reference than separate bespoke studies, while the founder has relevant EEG and analytics expertise. No measured price, speed, quality, recruitment-access, or benchmark-utility advantage is shown relative to established providers, and consortium governance adds buyer friction.

factors.name: Timing and momentum
factors.rationale: Wearable validation and digital-measurement infrastructure create a reasonable underlying context, but the packet identifies no immediate catalyst specific to this consortium. EHDS is permit-based and its relevant clinical-study and cohort provisions phase in later, so it does not supply the near-term access or exclusivity tailwind that might otherwise strengthen timing.

factors.name: Distribution
factors.rationale: The proposed bounded sale is identifiable, but it requires at least two noncompeting sponsors to align on endpoint, schedule, deposits, and benchmark terms while a clinic team also commits. There is no signed channel, lead pipeline, measured sales cycle, or anchor sponsor, and this trust-heavy multi-party sale is poorly matched to the founder's limited time and social-energy preference unless a partner owns much of it.

factors.name: Execution and risks
factors.rationale: The founder is well suited to protocol analytics and productization, and explicit no-go gates reduce downside before participant operations begin. Success still requires qualified clinical leadership, ethics and regulatory navigation, GDPR-compliant rights, recruitment, signal quality, participant support, sponsor contracting, and capital coordination that AI cannot replace; none of the essential external commitments is secured.

highest_value_structural_change: Replace the initial two-sponsor consortium dependency with a clinic- or CRO-channel partnership and one anchor sponsor that fully funds a private, fixed-endpoint pilot under explicit permitted aggregate-data terms; add a second sponsor and shared benchmark product only after the protocol, economics, rights, and buyer utility have been demonstrated. This preserves the potential data asset while reducing simultaneous launch dependencies and borrowing clinical trust and operations.
main_structural_strength: The opportunity converts a speculative cohort into a conditional, sponsor-precommitted protocol: funding, clinical responsibility, regulatory route, and lawful reuse rights must all be documented before major capital or participant exposure, while repeat standardized work could eventually create a compounding benchmark asset.
primary_score_limiter: The commercial engine is an unproven multi-party coordination sale: the business cannot launch unless multiple sponsors share an endpoint and timing, prepay enough to cover external costs, a clinic accepts regulated responsibilities, and contracts permit useful pooled derivatives, all while established providers offer credible alternatives.
strongest_disconfirming_evidence: VivoSense, Empatica, TNO, and Delve already market overlapping end-to-end wearable-study, device-integration, validation, regulatory, quality-control, and participant-operation capabilities, directly weakening the claim that this consortium has a sufficiently distinct or dominant offer; the packet provides no buyer evidence of an unmet Central-European gap to offset that competition.
